summary:
The 15Al alloy is the Fe-35Mn-15Al-5Cu (at.%) Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel, obtained by vacuum induction melting, homogenization (1200 °C/24 h), hot rolling to 4 mm plate, and EDM cutting into 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 coupons. This particular sample is the state produced by solution treatment at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon followed by oil quenching and then aging at 600 °C for 3 h with a final water quench. It is one of the ultra-high-hardness states of the 15Al alloy, reaching 938.2 ± 18.0 HV through the near-complete α → β-Mn transformation that is already finished within about 1 h at 600 °C, and it belongs to a study of how Al content controls the aging-hardening behavior of Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels.</summary>
<parameter name="composition">Nominally Fe-35Mn-15Al-5Cu (at.%). EDS-measured composition (Table 1) is Fe 44.6, Mn 35.2, Al 15.0, Cu 5.2 at.%; across the alloy series the Al variation from 15.0 to 18.6 at.% is achieved by substituting Al for Fe while Mn (35.2) and Cu (5.2 at.%) stay essentially constant. Design intent: the high Mn content of 35 at.% is chosen to accelerate the precipitation kinetics of the hard β-Mn phase that is responsible for the ultra-high and flexible hardness; Al is the primary density-reducing element (about 1 wt.% Al lowers the density by roughly 0.1 g/cm3) and also influences β-Mn precipitation and hardening; Cu is added because it promotes the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn and enhances hardness. The density of the 15Al alloy measured by the Archimedes method is 6.85 g/cm3.
processing: Ingots of nominal Fe-35Mn-xAl-5Cu (at.%, x = 15, 17, 19) were produced by vacuum induction melting of high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials under an argon atmosphere. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h and hot-rolled into 4 mm thick plates. These plates were cut by electrical discharge machining (EDM) into 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 samples for hardness testing and microstructure characterization. All samples were then solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere followed by oil quenching; this solution treatment (proc_st-1100c-10min-oq) is the parent process of the present sample. The solution-treated 15Al samples were subsequently aged at 600 °C for 3 h and water quenched, which is the terminal state of process proc_aging-600c-3h. Across the study, aging was explored between 525 °C and 650 °C for 1, 3, 6 and 10 h, with all aging treatments ending in water quenching.
microstructure: The solution-treated starting state is a single α (BCC) phase — no γ (FCC) is resolved in the phase maps. On aging at 600 °C the α matrix of the 15Al alloy transforms almost completely into β-Mn within about 1 h, so the 600 °C/3 h state is a near-completely transformed β-Mn matrix rather than a partially reacted α + β-Mn mixture. β-Mn generally precipitates as a short rod-shaped phase along α grain boundaries and inside α grains and grows until the precipitates contact one another. Within the β-Mn, abundant fine precipitates are present and are identified by EBSD as a new fine BCC phase and an FCC Cu-rich phase. The FCC Cu-rich precipitates are enriched in Cu, depleted in Fe and Mn and slightly poor in Al, and they form at the β-Mn interfaces; β-Mn itself is rich in Mn and poor in Al and Cu. The overall phase-evolution sequence during aging of the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu steels is α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase. Note that no EBSD/SEM/TEM panel maps this exact 600 °C/3 h condition for the 15Al alloy: the 15Al EBSD work used 525 °C/3 h, 550 °C/6 h and 650 °C/3 h, the SEM matrix covered 525-575 °C (1, 3, 6, 10 h) plus 600 °C-1 h, 600 °C-6 h, 625 °C-1 h and 650 °C-1 h, and the TEM study was performed on the 15Al alloy aged at 600 °C/6 h (the 965.6 HV peak condition). The microstructure assigned here therefore rests on the reported generic behavior of the 15Al alloy at 600 °C and above.
properties: Vickers microhardness of this condition is 938.2 ± 18.0 HV (Table 2), measured on 10 × 5 × 2 mm3 specimens with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester under a 9.8 N load for 15 s, each sample tested five times and averaged. For context, the 600 °C aging series of the 15Al alloy is the highest of all temperatures studied, hardening above 900 HV already at 3 h and peaking at 965.6 ± 7.6 HV at 6 h (a sibling condition); the solution-treated baseline is 253.4 ± 2.1 HV, so the 600 °C/3 h state sits far along the ultra-high-hardness plateau. The elastic modulus of the 15Al alloy determined from compressive stress-strain curves is 164 GPa. Characterization techniques applied to the 15Al alloy include Vickers microhardness testing, XRD (D8 Discover), SEM secondary-electron/EDS (ZEISS Sigma 300, 5 kV), EBSD (GeminiSEM 300, step size 1.5 μm low magnification and 0.05 μm high magnification), TEM/SAED/HRTEM/EDS (FEI Talos F200X, 200 kV), and nanoindentation (Agilent G200). No condition-specific micrograph or additional mechanical test is reported for the 600 °C/3 h state itself.
mechanisms: Ultra-high hardness originates mainly from the extensive, continuous precipitation of the ultra-hard β-Mn phase: the β-Mn has an intrinsic hardness above 10 GPa (12.1 ± 0.3 GPa for the hardest 15Al sample), so the α → β-Mn transformation converts a soft 253.4 HV solution-treated matrix into an ultra-hard one.

At 600 °C the α matrix transforms almost completely to β-Mn within just ~1 h, because raising the aging temperature increases both the driving force for β-Mn formation and the atomic diffusion rate; this is why the 600 °C/3 h state is already on the ultra-high-hardness plateau (938.2 HV) whereas at 525-550 °C the same hardening needs 6 h or more.

The high Mn content (35 at.%) is the design lever that speeds up β-Mn precipitation kinetics, since β-Mn is an Mn-rich phase whose nucleation and growth require Mn enrichment with rejection of Fe, Al and Cu into the surrounding matrix; the Cu addition further promotes β-Mn precipitation kinetics and raises hardness.

The fine precipitates that form inside/at the interfaces of β-Mn arise from elemental partitioning during the α → β-Mn transformation: Fe, Al and Cu are expelled from the Mn-rich β-Mn, so Al enrichment around β-Mn interfaces stabilizes the new BCC phase, while the limited solubility of Cu in Fe-based alloys causes the Cu-rich FCC phase to form.

Hardness of the ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu steels depends not only on the intrinsic hardness of β-Mn but also on its absolute volume fraction, because the FCC Cu-rich and BCC phases at the β-Mn interfaces have lower intrinsic hardness than β-Mn; a higher content of these softer interface precipitates lowers the overall hardness.

Increasing Al content slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn and raises the aging temperature/time needed for complete transformation, because more Al atoms must be rejected around the growing Mn-rich β-Mn, and because the Al-rich D0 3 phase, whose amount/size and stability grow with Al, has to be depleted before β-Mn can nucleate and grow.
conclusions: Within the parent study, the 600 °C/3 h condition belongs to the highest-aging-temperature plateau of the 15Al alloy: at 600 °C and above the α → β-Mn transformation of 15Al is complete within about 1 h, giving an ultra-high hardness of 938.2 ± 18.0 HV at 3 h and the series maximum of 965.6 HV at 6 h. The 15Al alloy has the fastest β-Mn precipitation kinetics and the highest hardening response of the three Al contents studied — its optimal ultra-high-hardness aging window is mainly 525-600 °C, compared with 550-600 °C for 17Al and 575-625 °C for 19Al — so increasing Al content shifts the optimum to higher temperature and slightly lowers the achievable peak hardness. The combination of ultra-high hardness and low density gives the Fe-35.2Mn-15.0Al-5.2Cu alloy an ultra-high specific hardness of 141 HV·cm3/g, the highest among the plotted low-density steels, conventional steels, pure iron and medium/high-entropy alloys, while its fracture toughness at peak hardness (8.6 MPa·m1/2) remains acceptable relative to the higher-Al siblings. Practically, the simple short-time aging route lets the alloy be formed in the soft solution-treated state and then aged to a chosen hardness within a very wide 253.4-965.6 HV window, enabling "one material, multiple uses" for lightweight structural components while saving fabrication time and cost; the residual limitation is that toughness is still not good enough, so the hardness-toughness trade-off needs further study.
